items.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007
items.q: I got the record player and started playing the Louis Armstrong records... I listened to those Armstrong records enough to begin to memorize them... I wanted to be a blues player, that was all I cared about, to play the blues, that’s all I wanted to do was play the blues, like Louis Armstrong.

ctx.x: Was he happy that you chose music as your career path?

He was kind of surprised about the whole thing. I did it without his — I mean he didn’t steer me to it. I did it sort of on my own. I was — when we went to San Antonio he put a collection of his — his 78 collection, which had gone to Venezuela and come back and many of the records had gotten broken in the process, but they were in a wooden chest and were temporarily in a small rent house, they were stuck in my little cubbyhole bedroom, that was the only place they would really fit. And we didn’t even have a…

everyday after school I’d come home and listen to the Bix Beiderbecke records, and I memorized a whole bunch of those. So that was the way I got into the music as a performing musician, it was very unorthodox. Because I was able to have all this music in my mind, I could sing these Armstrong and Beiderbecke solos and before I ever had any instrument or any instruction or anything, I already had this music in my head.
